newsitem.title: EGYPT: Doubts about 1997 Mideast conference start early.
newsitem.headline: Doubts about 1997 Mideast conference start early.

text.p: The season for doubts about the annual Middle East economic conference has come early this year and without a change in Israeli policy the Gulf state of Qatar may well have to call the meeting off, diplomats say.

Saudi Arabia has said it will not attend the conference in November. Other important Arab states, including Egypt and Morocco, have decided to wait and see whether anything happens in peace talks between Israel and the Palestinians.

In a repetition of the wrangling before last year's conference in Cairo, the United States is leaning on its Arab allies to go ahead with the meeting but this year it will not be so easy to win them over, the diplomats say.

"We encourage all Arab countries to participate in the Doha economic summit," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said on Wednesday. "Those Arab governments who said they won't attend, we hope they'll reconsider their positions."
The conferences, launched in Casablanca in 1994, are meant to promote peace in the Middle East through trade and economic cooperation between Israel and its Arab neighbours.
Egypt came close to cancelling the Cairo conference for fear that the recently elected right-wing government in Israel would scare away many of the potential participants.
"What you're seeing now is much the same as last year but it's a bit earlier and a bit noisier," one diplomat said.
"It's more serious this year because of Abu Ghneim and the atmosphere between Israel and the Palestinians," he added.
Jabal Abu Ghneim, a site in Arab East Jerusalem known to Israelis as Har Homa, has become the symbol for deadlock in Israeli-Palestinian negotiations.
The talks broke down in March when the government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu decided to go ahead with plans to build a Jewish settlement on the site.
Egyptian mediators have tried to patch up a compromise but, without strong support from the United States to lean on the Israeli side, nothing has come of their endeavours.
Washington's reluctance to press hard for progress has helped erode its influence over the Arab states, diplomats say.
Diplomats in the Gulf states, which are crucial to the fate of this year's Doha conference, are resisting with unusual vigour U.S. pressure to talk trade with the Israelis.

"There is a general feeling that they (the Gulf states) can easily live without any economic or business benefits from this conference and making a point about the need to make progress in the peace process is more important at this stage," a diplomat in the Saudi capital Riyadh said this week.

Arab public opinion is overwhelmingly hostile to economic cooperation with Israelis and a conference this year would sit ill with an Arab decision in March to suspend the steps they have taken towards normal ties with the Jewish state.
For the moment, the Qataris say they are going ahead with preparations for the meeting, regardless of Arab reservations.
"Our main concern at present is to make arrangements for the summit and we are going ahead with it," Minister of State for Foreign Affairs, Ahmad Abdullah al-Mahmood, said on Wednesday.
Asked whether Israel would be invited, Mahmood said: "As of now, we are only occupied with making arrangements. Invitations will go out only a few weeks before the summit date".
But Saudi Arabia, the dominant state in the Gulf, appears to have taken a final decision not to take part.

"We told them (the Qataris) this conference will harm them and we advised them that we and most Arabs will not attend," Saudi Crown Prince Abdullah said last week. "We advised them to drop this conference," he added.

Saudi Foreign Minister Saud al-Faisal, arriving in Cairo for talks with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak on Thursday, said: "The crown prince's statements were clear in this matter and it is not for me to add to what he said."
"It is Israeli policy that threatens not only the peace process but the method followed in the context of the peace process, including the...multilateral negotiations," he added.

The economic conferences, though sponsored by the Swiss-based World Economic Forum from 1994 onwards, have become part of the multilateral process launched at the Middle East peace conference in Madrid in 1991.

Diplomats in Cairo said tiny Qatar would find it harder than Egypt last year to attract reluctant Arabs. The Gulf state also has less to gain than Egypt, which turned the Cairo meeting into a vehicle for promoting its own investment opportunities.
But they said anything could happen in Israeli politics over the next few months so it was too early to write Doha off.
"There might be a change of government, negotiations might move ahead at full steam. Under those circumstances, the conference would happen," one diplomat said.
